prime.problem: Two numbers (a mean and a variance) don't pin down a distribution, and getting moments from a pmf by summing series is slow. You need one object that carries the whole distribution and gives moments by differentiation.
prime.fits: The first card on distributions. The convolution card showed that the generating function of an independent sum is the product; the MGF is the same tool with z = eᵗ. Every distribution card after this one has an MGF column you can now read.
expect: uniqueness: equal MGFs mean equal distributions
trials against failures: the eᵗ on top
prime.goal: Read a pmf off a finite MGF, get moments by differentiating at 0, and name a closed-form MGF by matching it to the catalogue.

attend: Why is the coefficient of e<sup>tx</sup> exactly P(X = x), and what does M(0) = 1 check?
Why does differentiating once and setting t = 0 turn each term into x·p(x)?
Why doesn't matching the mean and variance prove you have the right distribution, when matching the MGF does?
Which single feature of (0.7/(1 − 0.3eᵗ))⁵ tells you it counts failures, not trials?

must: M(t) = Σ p(x)e<sup>tx</sup> → the multiplier of t in each exponent is a value and its coefficient is that value's probability → a finite MGF is the pmf written another way
d/dt brings x down from e<sup>tx</sup> → at t = 0, e⁰ = 1 → M′(0) = Σ x p(x) = E[X] and M″(0) = E[X²] → Var = M″(0) − M′(0)² = 6 − 49/9 = 5/9
An MGF that is finite near 0 determines the distribution → match the whole function to a catalogue entry → naming NB(5, 0.7) is then a proof, not a guess
Independent sum → the MGFs multiply → a geometric MGF to the 5th power is NB(5, p), and Poisson exponents add
elevated: Trials and failures differ by an eᵗ in the numerator → shifting X by r multiplies M by e<sup>rt</sup> → the mean moves from 15/7 to 50/7, and the variance stays 150/49
reference: the catalogue of MGFs (look them up)
the characteristic function E[e<sup>itX</sup>] for heavy tails
the PGF G(s) = E[s<sup>X</sup>], with M(t) = G(eᵗ)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences the three things you can do with an MGF (read, differentiate, match), then redo problem 1's mean and variance on paper.
checklist: each term p(x)e<sup>tx</sup> is one value with its probability
the n-th derivative at 0 is the n-th moment
uniqueness makes a match a proof
sums of independent variables multiply their MGFs
an eᵗ on top means the trials convention

retrieve.q: Explain why a coin flip between 1.588 and 3.079 is not problem 1's Y, even though its mean and variance match.
answer: two moments don't determine a distribution
the coin takes two values; Y takes 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/6, 1/3, 1/2
their MGFs differ, and only equal MGFs (finite near 0) guarantee the same distribution

retrieve.q: Walk through getting E[X] and Var(X) from M(t) = (0.2 + 0.8eᵗ)⁴, and name the distribution.
Catalogue match, series expansion or finite differences: when is each worth doing?
answer: catalogue match: seconds, and a proof if the whole function matches
series expansion: gives the pmf itself and proves the match, but costs minutes by hand
finite differences: a numeric check of the moments when the derivative is messy, never exact

compare.q: This card names NB(5, 0.7) from its MGF; the negative-binomial card builds it from five geometrics. What does each route show that the other hides?
answer: the MGF match proves the identity quickly but doesn't say what is being counted
the build shows the story: five geometric waits laid end to end
the build also explains the fifth power: five independent pieces, so five MGFs multiply

compare.q: The generating function in z against the MGF in t: what is the same, and when is each one handier?
answer: M(t) = G(eᵗ): the same object, and both multiply for independent sums
G(z) is handier for counts, because P(X = k) is the coefficient of zᵏ
M(t) is handier for moments (derivatives at 0) and also works for non-integer values

compare.q: The MGF of a sum against the MGF of a product: why does the multiplication rule apply to one and not the other?
answer: sum: e<sup>t(X+Y)</sup> = e<sup>tX</sup>e<sup>tY</sup>, and independence splits the expectation
you condition on one factor and average instead, so MGFs are the tool for sums, not products

predict.q: M(t) = e<sup>3(eᵗ − 1)</sup> · (1/3 + (2/3)eᵗ). What are E[X] and Var(X), and what is X? Commit first.
predict.answer: X is Poisson(3) plus an independent Bernoulli(2/3): the MGF is the product of the two catalogue MGFs. E[X] = 3 + 2/3 = 11/3 and Var = 3 + (2/3)(1/3) = 29/9. A product of MGFs is a sum of independent variables.

apply.task: Write the MGF of a fair die, Σ ekt/6, and get E and Var with moments_from_terms. Then build the MGF of the sum of two dice by multiplying the term dictionaries, and read P(sum = 7) off the coefficient of e7t.
apply.done: The die gives 7/2 and 35/12 (as on the uniform card). For two dice the e7t coefficient is 6/36 = 1/6, and moments_from_terms on the product gives mean 7 and variance 35/6.
apply.hint: Multiplying two sums of e<sup>kt</sup> terms adds the exponents: loop over both dictionaries and accumulate c<sub>1</sub>c<sub>2</sub> at key k<sub>1</sub> + k<sub>2</sub>.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the name of the product MGF, or its variance?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why derivatives at 0 give moments, or why uniqueness makes a match a proof?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: product of MGFs → sum of variables, or eᵗ on top → trials?
Would you have spotted the trials/failures difference in an exam without the side-by-side table?
What will you revisit before the negative-binomial card?
